speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
These questions are difficult to answer. As to the first, no formal request has been made to the government with respect to the sale or export of power, but Mr. Sweezey, in the course of conversations, and other people as well, I fancy connected with the enterprise, have made the statement that they thought electrical energy could be sold in the United States. Therefore to answer "yes" or "no" would be difficult.
No formal permission to export power has been given, nor has any request been made formally for permission to export power to the United States. In any event the provisions of provincial statutes preclude the possibility of it being conveyed across highways or public places. Neither this, nor any government as far as I know, is in the habit of stating policy in respect of matters before the conditions necessitating the question of jurisdiction arise.
As to the fourth question, the government does not propose at the present time to submit the question to the privy council.
To the question relating to the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, the answer is much more difficult. There were statements made from time to time, but the correspondence that was brought down at the last session clearly indicates the extent to which they assumed any definite form, as to the possibility of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company taking over the Beauharnois enterprise in September, 1931. In view of the fact that from time to time all the correspondence of importance has been tabled and that the motion that stands in the hon. gentleman's name asks that the balance of the correspondence be brought down, I do not think I can answer the question except in the manner indicated.

The house resumed from Friday, March 10, 'onsideration of the motion of Hon. R. J. Manion for the second reading of Bill No. 37, respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for cooperation with the Canadian Pacific railway system, and for other purposes.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few remarks on this question I am fully conscious of the fact, after listening to the very excellent speeches which have been made by hon. members in all corners of the house, that one taking part in the debate at this time cannot very well cover any new ground and must repeat, though perhaps not in the same words, many things , that have been said already. However, I believe this debate to be one of the most important that we have had in this house for some years, because it opens up the whole question of transportation facilities in this country, a question which vitally concerns every taxpayer in Canada. Therefore, with the indulgence of the house, I should like to add a few remarks to what has been said previously.
In passing I should like to commend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), as other members have done, for the tone of his address in introducing the bill now before the house. He placed the debate on a very high plane, if I may say so, and I shall endeavour to follow him in that regard.
I should like to say first, Mr. Speaker, that the history of railroad construction in this young vigorous country in some respects does not make very good reading. Undoubtedly mistakes have been made. There have been not only errors in judgment on the part of some railway promoters; there have been errors in judgment, if you like, by previous governments both Liberal and Conservative. I am not going to dwell upon that aspect of the case because I have not sufficient time at my disposal, but for a moment or two I should like to direct my remarks to the present position of our railway companies. To-day in this country we have two great railway companies. One is privately owned, well managed and well financed; it has served

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Sanderson
the people of this country in a very efficient way for a great many years. The other day the Prime Minister stated that the securities of the Canadian Pacific Railway were held not only in Canada but also in the United States, in Great Britain and in almost every country in the world, and those securities always have held a high place in the financial markets of the world. We must admit that when this great railway was being constructed it received very substantial aid from the country, not only by way of money but also by way of large grants of land. I do not take exception to that, because this was a pioneer company which did wonderful work in building this railway line from one end of this country to the other. As a matter of fact I am free to admit-though I hold no brief for the Canadian Pacific Railway-that at present, despite the fact that during the last two or three years its earnings have been depleted because of world economic conditions, it stands to-day as perhaps one of the best managed privately owned railway companies in the world, and it has done a great deal to develop Canada and to advertise this country all over the world.
Side by side with this great privately owned company we have what is known as the people's railway, the Canadian National system. I am not going back to the time when the companies which now make up the Canadian National system were taken over by the government of the day; the other day the Prime Minister went into this question very fully. But I do not want to forget, and I do not believe the people of Canada will forget, that this conglomeration of bankrupt railways, if I may so term them, which were wished on this country and which now comprise the Canadian National system, were taken over by the government at a time when a decision had to be made as to whether the country would clean the slate and take its huge losses in money which had been advanced to these roads, or would take them over and run them as a publicly owned1 and publicly controlled road. I am not going into that phase of the question but, Mr. Speaker, as I believe the Canadian Pacific system is one of the outstanding privately owned railways in the world so I believe that the system owned and controlled by this country stands out as one of the best managed and best organized publicly owned railways in the world, despite the fact that it is going through heavy weather at the present time.
We have, then, Mr. Speaker, these two great competing railway systems, and sometimes I think we do not realize their immensity. In round figures the Canadian Pacific Railway has in Canada some sixteen thousand miles of track,
in addition to which it controls a certain mileage in the United States. The Canadian National system owns about twenty-two thousand miles of track in Canada, in round figures, and also controls some mileage in the United States. These two railway corporations control about 40,000 miles of track and have employed in normal times, the two together, about 190,000 men. In normal times they have paid out in salaries and wages to employees as large a sum as $290,000,000 a year. That will give some idea of the immensity of the business carried on by the two great railway systems of Canada. They have both been successful until the present period of depression struck this country in common with the rest of the world.
I have nothing but praise both for the Canadian Pacific Railway and for the Canadian National, except in one regard. I have always been of the opinion that the management of both railways were very slow in attempting to cope with a new form of competition that has entered the field, competition of enormous magnitude, namely, the commercial motor truck. In my opinion this motor truck competition when it first appeared could have been combated by the railways if they had put their own trucks into operation. Had they done this at the outset of this competition the earnings of both railways would have been augmented by many millions of dollars during the last twelve or fifteen years. Apart from this, however, I think that the management has been excellent in both cases.
I hold no brief for Sir Henry Thornton, and perhaps he made mistakes. But for that matter who has not made mistakes in every business, in every walk of life, during the good times we had in this country for a number of years? I will say this, however, in praise of Sir Henry Thornton. In the number of years during which he was president and general manager of the Canadian National Railways his achievements far outnumbered any mistakes he ever made. There was a time when the earnings of the Canadian National system were piling up, when that system went after business and got it, and when the morale of its thousands of employees was at its highest owing to the example set them by their chief, Sir Henry Thornton. At that time no one in this country would dare to get up and say that Sir Henry Thornton was not making a success of th'e Canadian National Railways; but when conditions began to get bad, when tonnage declined, when business was poor, then the criticism started. The Prime Minister himself gave Sir Henrjr Thornton a good deal

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Sill-Mr. Sanderson
of credit a few years ago. It will be remembered that in 1926 there was a general election in Canada. The present Prime Minister was then Minister of Finance in Mr. Meighen's government-someone says the shadow government. Be that as it may, he was Minister of Finance in that government and during that election campaign to which I have just referred he made several speeches in western Ontario. He went to the city of Stratford in the county of Perth, which is a large divisional point on the Canadian National roads. Many hundreds of railwaymen live there, there are big car shops there, and it is perhaps as important a divisional point as any other in the whole system. The then Minister of Finance in Mr. Meighen's government addressed a meeting in the city of Stratford on the evening of August 14, 1926, for the benefit of the Conservative candidate. He was addressing an audience in which there were hundreds of Canadian National railway employees on whom naturally he wanted to make a good impression, with a view if possible to winning them over for the Conservative candidate. This is what he said then in regard to the Canadian National Railways:
Mr. Bennett denounced in scathing terms the whispering campaign about the Canadian National Railways, saying that Mr. Meighen had always fought for the road, and had no intention of interfering with its management. In that connection he said that he personally had recommended to Mr. King that Sir Henry Thornton be hired to operate the road. This he had done_ as a result of information from Mr. Thomas in England, he said, and indicated that he thought Sir Henry Thornton had been successful and that his work would certainly not be interfered with by Mr. Meighen.
Merely for information, may I ask the hon. member what he is quoting from.

I expected that the
Minister of Railways would ask that question and I am happy to be able to inform him. This is an absolutely correct report which appeared in three newspapers at the time. The meeting was held on Saturday, the 14th, and this report appeared in the Toronto Globe on August 16, 1926; in the Stratford Beacon-Herald on August 16, 1926; and-I know that this will please the Minister of Railways and he will take it for granted^ in the London Free Press on August 16, 1926. So that it is official.
I find no fault with the remarks of the then Minister of Finance in Mr. Meighen's government, but I am inclined to think that he has since had a change of heart.
He certainly has.

An hon. gentleman
says he has, and I accept that. In 1926 the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister apparently not only praised Sir Henry Thornton but wished to get on the band wagon and get all the credit for himself, for he said that he really was the man who had chosen Sir Henry Thornton and had been instrumental in bringing him here. This newspaper report which I have just quoted [DOT]declares that the right hon. gentleman denounced in scathing terms the whispering campaign in regard to the Canadian National Railways. Well, if there was a whispering campaign then in this country there are more than whisperings at the present time. The Prime Minister last Thursday, in the course of his speech in this debate, virtually said that the Canadian National railway system was bankrupt, and instead of joining in a whispering campaign he almost made an
S.O.S. call for the undertaker to bury the whole _ road. I mention this to show the inconsistency between the remarks of the Prime Minister to-day and the statements which he made when he was Minister of Finance in Mr. Meighen's government, when he spoke in the election campaign of 1926.
I will refer now for a moment or two to the royal commission, the so-called Duff commission, who have laboured and brought in this report upon which is founded the bill now under discussion. The commission was composed of seven gentlemen, all very eminent in their own spheres. I have gone through the report of this commission as carefully as possible and the only conclusion I can arrive at is that after holding eighteen meetings, lasting fifty days and travelling over nearly all the main lines of both these railway systems, they have not told us anything about these railroads which we did not already know. They have told us nothing that the Minister of Railways did not know; they have told us nothing that the right hon. the Prime Minister did not know, they have told us nothing that every hon. member of this house and almost every man in the whole dominion did not know. I shall not take up the time of the house in reading the conclusions of the commission because I suppose every hon. member has read them. All through their report these gentlemen seem to be leaning towards the amalgamation of these two roads. They do not say so in so many words but that is the inference I draw from their report. I want to be fair to the members of this royal commission but as a member of this house I think I have the right to criticize their report if I so desire and my criticism is that most of the gentle-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Sanderson
men who composed this commission were in favour of privately owned rather than publicly owned railroads. The report bears out my contention. I repeat, this commission after having gone up and down this country, have not told us anything new. They did make certain recommendations which are embodied in the bill now before us, in the discussion of which I shall take a few minutes.
The -bill is divided into three parts. I am only a layman and could not go into the legal aspects of the bill, but I have endeavoured to study it with an entirely open mind. Part I of the bill deals with the substitution of three trustees or receivers, as the Prime Minister chooses to call them, for the seventeen directors and general manager who have been administering the affairs of this road for some years. These trustees are given absolute powers in the administration of the affairs of the Canadian National system. They are to be given powers which in my judgment should not be given to any three men. They will be a law unto themselves, they will not be responsible to parliament or to the taxpayers of this country who have been paying the deficits of the Cariadian National road. They will be able to do just as they like for a period of seven years. It is true that they can be removed from office by an address to the House of Commons and the Senate but that course would never be taken. They will be vested with authority and responsibilities which should not be vested in any three men no matter how capable they may be, no matter what business sagacity they may possess. It is too much power to be given to any trustees or to any body of men. The Prime Minister said that they would be more receivers than trustees. I was a little puzzled at that definition and I looked up the legal meaning of a receiver. I found that a receiver is a person appointed ordinarily by a court of equitable jurisdiction to receive and hold in trust money or other property pending suit, in the case of a person incompetent to manage his own property or upon the winding up or dissolution of a partnership or corporation. A receiver is an officer of the court and the property held by him is not subject to process other than in the case itself. A receiver often obtains authority to continue to manage the business as a going concern.
These three receivers are to administer the affairs of the Canadian National system for the people of this country for at least the next seven years. As I said before, they are to be vested with authority which should not be vested in any one man or in any three men. They are to be a law unto themselves.
I cannot understand why three receivers- that is what the Prime Minister calls them- should be called in at this stage to administer the affairs of this railway. It is the most peculiar receivership of which I have ever heard.
In addition to providing for the appointment of these three receivers, the bill provides for compulsory cooperation or, as the Prime Minister said the other day, directed cooperation between tbje Canadian -Pacific and the Canadian National roads. What kind of amalgamation is this to be? They will not be joined in wedlock but they will be handcuffed and shackled together. The Canadian National is to be administered by three trustees and by a president who is to be the operating manager. This president is not to be responsible to the Minister of Railways, he is not to be responsible to this parliament, lie is to be responsible only to the three trustees. The purport of this bill is to join these two great railroads together and, as I said, handcuff them and shackle them and keep them in that position for seven years.
A study of the history of the railroads of the United States will show that during the war the government administered the railroads, although at the moment I cannot say whether this was done under trustees, receivers or just what form of control was used. But the result of the control vested in private individuals by the government was that they made bankrupt every railroad which they were permitted to manage. That has been the history of trusteeship or receivership, if you like, in the United States. While I do not want to be pessimistic; while I do not want to make any prophecies as to the future, I am of opinion that if this bill goes into effect, one of three things will happen within the next seven years. One will be that we shall have complete amalgamation of these two railways, either the absorption of the Canadian Pacific by the publicly owned road or the absorption of the publicly owned by the privately owned road, or both roads will be so impaired, so restricted in business that this will constitute one of the biggest calamities Canada has ever experienced.
The very conclusions at which the royal commission- arrived in regard to economy and cutting down of expenses have been put into effect during the last two years. This started before the royal commission began to function and it has been continuing. Mr. Speaker, the railway situation in the Dominion of Canada is, I am free to admit, rather serious, but not more serious than that of other industries. We are not discussing this bill and this question to-day solely because of the railway situation. We are studying it largely because of the tremendous worldwide economic depression of which Canada has experienced her full share, due partly to her own policies, partly to policies in other countries and partly to other factors. We have had in the last four years a shrinkage of about 50 per cent in world trade. The British note mailed to Washington last December referred to the depression as one of unparalleled severity. It has been called an economic blizzard and several other names indicating that most people thought it was the worst depression we ever had. The report of the committee on transportation calls attention to this as being one of the contributing factors but the railway problem is not any more serious than the agricultural, the manufacturing or the financial question or that of government, federal, provincial and municipal, with regard to deficits, and unless we can get some other commission or some other means of dealing with the depression as it affects other industries, it is not worth while dealing with this bill or trying to do anything with the railways; we are heading for disaster. Personally, I do not think we are heading towards a disaster although we have already experienced something which might be termed that. I believe that to-day and during the last few years the world has been learning lessons which will be of immense value in the future. When one studies all the troubles confronting the world, considers the position of industry generally,

and the economic life of this and other countries, one feels as though all the waves and billows have gone over it.
Some of the speeches made in the house have indicated that members are under the impression that the trouble is due to extravagance. To some degree I share the views of hon. members who have spoken kindly concerning Sir Henry Thornton, and yet in my judgment in the last eight or nine years some inexcusable things have been done. There was extravagance shown by the railways in the building of hotels, in the development of steamships, and passenger services. But, Mr. Speaker, those were not the factors which made the real railway problem, if we want to discuss it as a problem distinct from all others. The railway problem in Canada was made previous to the war, and any hon. member who has doubts in the matter would do well to read the Drayton-Acworth commission report of 1917. Anyone who considers that report carefully must come to the conclusion that it was what happened previous to 1914, the excess mileage built in those years and the railways planned during that period, which is responsible for the real railway difficulties from which we suffer to-day. Among other things that report states that Canada had room for two transcontinental systems, but not for -three. I believe that is the chief problem. If hon. members would examine the evidence submitted to the commission and study the report prepared by three gentlemen, one from the United States and two from the Department of Finance, they will find that the duplications set out as being unnecessary were duplications of transcontinental mileage mainly, and have nothing to do with branch lines.
There is of course another reason for our great surprise to-day. Is is that no one

They were caught as much by surprise as were the farmer and his hired man, the bricklayer or the hodcarrier. And if anything has tended to make me lose faith in supermen it is my study of this question. When I was very young I lost faith in Santa Claus. A little later in l-ife I gave up hero-worship. To-day certainly I have lost the last vestige of faith in supermen. They are a relic of barbarism and superstition belonging to the age of tribal medicine men and witch doctors.
You have lost faith even in prime ministers?
It applies to all supermen.
Would the hon. member go as far as to say that all the supermen are in the soup?

Between the years 1904 and 1917 the railway mileage in Canada was doubled. During those years we completed mileages ranging from 514 miles in one year up to about 5,000 miles in another. During the years following 1923 we built a few hundred miles annually. I challenge anybody to show that the branch lines built since 1923 loaded the Canadian National Railways or the Canadian Pacific Railway with anything which might be described as a real financial problem. The Duff report calls attention to the fact that we have less population per mile of railroad than has any other country in the world. That is only a half truth. Canada stands twenty-third in the list of countries, so far as population is concerned. China is at the top with a population of 444,000,000 and Canada comes in twenty-third along with Ethiopia and the Belgian Congo with 10,000,000. But where is Canada with respect to export trade? In 1929 the United States was at the top, with the United Kingdom running a close second, Germany third, France fourth and Canada fifth. Speaking before the royal commission, Mr. Ilungerford, the acting president of the Canadian National Railways, pointed out that while between the years 1900 and 1929 the railway mileage increased by 135 per cent, the gross earnings of railways in the same period increased 656 per cent and the external trade of the country increased by 645 per cent.
We all know that Canada's railways have been laid out with the idea in mind of a vast export trade. Canada is, and has been for a number of years, leading the world in the export of wheat, and our wheat area is located farther from the sea than the area of any other country exporting wheat to the great markets of the world. It is preposterous to state that because we have less population per mile of railroad than has any other country of the world, we are over-railroaded. That is but a half truth, and before we can thoroughly appraise the whole situation it

I listened to the remarks of the Minister of Railways, and I may say that I agreed pretty generally with what he had to say. However, he made one statement to which I should like to refer, because I do not know whether he meant it as it stands in Hansard. He went on to explain it later, but I noticed that one of the newspapers took this portion of his remarks and dealt with it as though it were quite separate. At page 2777 of Hansard for this session the minister said:
T must confess it was my own conviction-[DOT] that grain traffic was the paying traffic of the railways. As a matter of fact, it was not so much the wheat and grain traffic that was the paying traffic for the railways as the fact that the people of the west were selling their products at a reasonable price and had the money with which to purchase goods from some other section of the country, thus providing return traffic; and that total traffic brought about the prosperity of the railways.
Some of us have argued as to the importance to the railways of the wheat traffic, and the traffic in agricultural products generally, but I submit that no one from the west who has had enough knowledge of the subject to express an opinion ever thought that the wheat traffic was sufficiently profitable to carry the railways without other traffic. This, however, does bring out the fact .that the wheat crop is an originator of new wealth and new purchasing power, and unless the farmers can sell their products at a profit in the markets of the world there will be no real solution for the railway problem in this country for some years, at all events. It is remarkable how steady has been the planted wheat acreage of the west in the face of this shrinking price level, and the steadiness and dependability of the railway service throughout these years when the railway companies have been losing money has greatly contributed to the stability of the situation. I do wish that manufactur-[Mr. D. M. Kennedy.}
ing and financial concerns could give the same stability to the development and volume of trade and sales in spite of falling world prices; then we would not have the depression as severe as it is in Canada to-day. But, Mr. Speaker, the farmers have little or no control over the price level of wheat. I think, of course, that a reduction in the wheat acreage, if it could be effected in other countries as well, would help tremendously, and I think we should investigate that possibility. But I notice that the government is not throwing its weight in that direction at the present time. I want to say that the government, through whatever control it has over financial policies, has far more to do with price levels than the farmers have, and to the extent that they acted or did not act they must accept responsibility for the present condition. Any policies that have been adopted that interfere with the purchasing power of the farmers-whether those policies be tariffs or anything else-are contributing to the railway problem of this country. I know, of course, that a great deal of our trouble is world wide; I know the government has done something with regard to prices, but I mention these facts in passing.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the most important part of this bill is the section having to do with compulsory cooperation. I read the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and while I agree with some parts of it I cannot quite understand why it was brought forward at the time it was moved. When it comes to compulsory cooperation, however, I have been wondering if this principle was called to the attention of the hon member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNieol) and the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson). I have not much fear of communism or socialism or capitalism. I think the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) pointed out that what we had in Canada was a sort of mixture of cooperation and capitalism. I have not much fear of the theories which the ordinary individual has in the back of his head so long as he has common sense enough to know how far they can be applied in connection with the circumstances and affairs with

The manner in which hon. gentlemen have addressed themselves to this question, which is of such importance in this particularly critical time, is a matter of satisfaction not only to the house but to the country at large. The exposition of the railway situation as given by the leader of the government is worthy of the highest commendation, and the way in which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) set forth the facts will equally commend itself to this house when we remember the high plane on which he kept the discussion. Indeed, throughout this debate, so far, all hon. gentlemen who have spoken have endeavoured to keep the discussion on that same high plane. To my mind this emphasizes the seriousness of the problem with which we are confronted.
I feel disposed to support this measure for some half a dozen reasons. First and foremost to my mind is the fact that the putting of this legislation into effect will do more to arrest the possible collapse of our transportation system than any other piece of legislation that has come before the house in the last decade. Who is there in this chamber who will say that our transportation system was not headed for collapse had we continued to follow the policy of merciless competition and expansion which has been in vogue in the last ten years. The system was bound to collapse if we had continued along that line. We have had an example of what was bound to happen in what has happened to the country to the south of us in connection with another great national necessity; I refer to the collapse of the banking system there. The financial affairs of our railways are on a par with the banking system in importance and, I repeat, we were headed for collapse if action had not been taken.
The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) said a few moments ago that nothing was being done, that nothing new has come to light in this particular Duff report. He said that the Duff commission had only brought in evidence and information that we have all known for the last five or ten years. May I remind that hon. gentleman that during the last ten years his friends have been in power. If therefore they knew all these facts throughout that time why did they not initiate some legislation to 53719-187
prevent the collapse that was' inevitable? They had the benefit of the June 1925 report made by that impartial body the Senate. Did they take action on that report? They never did; they allowed the matter to drift. The hon. member also complained about a speech made by the present leader of the government in the city of Stratford, when the right hon. gentleman declared that if given power he would see that no harm would come to the Canadian National Railways. The Minister of Finance of that day knew, as members of the opposition to-day will no doubt recall, that the Senate had brought down a report indicating that something must be done to curb the reckless extravagance that was then taking place, and also emphasizing the importance of taking a grip on the situation and passing legislation of the kind we have before us to-day. The Senate had asked in their first recommendation that cooperation be made possible, and had we been given power at that time, instead of waiting another five years and spending another $500,000,000 of the taxpayer's money, this government would have seen to it that all that extravagance was avoided. I am satisfied that if this government. had been in power a good deal of the money would have been saved and, more than that, there would have been on the statute books of the country legislation similar to this, in accordance with that Senate report of 1925.
This legislation carries out the pledges given to the Canadian people by the party now in power. It is intended to conserve this great railway asset for the Canadian people, and one other bright spot is the assurance that it will prevent the situation from becoming, whenever there is an election in this country, nothing but a political football. It will tend to reconcile the opinions held on the one hand by those who believe in private ownership and on the other the opinions of those who support public ownership, and will avoid any serious divergence in their approach to this problem. It will re-establish confidence in the industries of our country, because from ten to fifty per cent of the cost of operating an industry is made up of transportation expenses and freight costs. Those engaged in industry know now that the government is firmly behind a movement towards retrenchment so far as unnecessary railway expenditures are concerned, and this in due course will reflect itself in freight rates on those commodities with which they carry on their business. Perhaps the most important aspect of all is that the large body of workmen whose vocation is on the railways of this country will now see that the government in power

is determined that neither the Canadian Pacific nor the Canadian National Railways shall fall into bankruptcy, and that these men's jobs will be assured them for some little time to come.
My hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) is concerned in this regard; he says that shops here, there and yon throughout the country will be closed down. He made the suggestion that from eight to ten thousand employees would find themselves out of work. I rather think the hon. gentleman is overdrawing the picture. He has a great love for his fellow men, and being of that Irish makeup you rather expect to find that in him. We do not look for that condition, rather we look for an improvement. Far be it from me to say that 20,000 out of the 150,000 are looking for some other vocation in life; the whole system will be demoralized if the 150,000 are not sure of their vocation. I think the men in the employ of these railways are satisfied that this government is going to do something to make the continuance of their jobs actually possible.
I come now to my seventh point. This legislation is the considered opinion of an impartial body which travelled this country from one end to the other in order to make a study of the problem. The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) has made the statement that nothinig new is contained in the report of the Duff commission, but I cannot agree with that statement. There were also the sittings of the Senate committee, another impartial body of men trained in business and from all walks of life, where

this matter was considered in an impartial manner and without political flavour. This bill now before us is the result of information which has been gathered during the past ten years. This information is to be found in the journals of the house, in the proceedings of the shipping committee, in the proceedings of the Senate committee of 1925, in the proceedings of the Duff commission and finally in the proceedings of the Senate committee of this year. All this information has been consolidated into this measure and it should receive the wholehearted support of this chamber.
I should like to make a few observations with regard to the loss of tonnage. Our primary commodities make up a large volume of the tonnage carried by our railways, but it is not always the most profitable tonnage. There is no gainsaying the fact that the low prices now offering for these commodities has retarded their movement. Because of low prices the primary producers find that in many cases it does not pay to send their goods to market. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Myers) gave an illustration the other evening when he referred to the difficulty in picking up potatoes here and there throughout Prince Edw'ard Island in order to move them to market. He referred to the inflexibility of our railroad classification. In the past our railroads have not adapted themselves to the difficulties faced by a sparsely populated country such as Canada. There is great difficulty in making up carload lots at points of origin, and this offers a big problem to the small shippers who produce only two or three ton lots of goods. The pooling arrangements and the cooperative measures contained within the four corners of this bill will make possible the pooling and loading of carload lots with a resultant benefit to the shipper.
During the past decade the one thought in the minds of the railroad men of America has been to build larger and heavier equipment. As an example, we have our 5700 engines with their 26 wheels. I am not complaining as we will have to do the best we can with them. We have our 100,000 pounds capacity freight cars weighing 40,000 pounds dead weight. I do not consider that such equipment is economical. Apparently the only thought in the minds of our railroad men is the movement of such bulk commodities as wheat, coal, and pulpwood. Did they consider the heavier units necessary to handle this heavy tonnage? I do not think sufficient consideration was given to the cost of the heavier rails, the extra foundation and roadbed and the stronger bridges necessary

to handle this type of equipment. There was also the necessity of installing heavier cranes, drills and lathes in the shops in order to handle the necessaiy repairs. In the past when thinking of freight we have been too prone to think only of wheat, coal, pulpwood, newsprint and similar heavier commodities; we seem to have lost sight of the fact that the real revenue producer is package freight. We are glad to have the wheat from the west which represents new wealth and all that, but is that the real revenue producer for the railroads? Is it not rather the package freight which is taken back to supply the needs of the primary producers?
I ask the house to bear with me for a moment while I discuss the industrial production in this country and its relation to freight rates. I should like to draw a line of demarcation between the type of industry which is prominently in the minds of certain economists, such as General Motors, the steel works at Sydney and Algoma and the pulp and paper mills, and those other industries which are the real backbone of the industrial life of this country. I refer to the small industries such as the shoe factories in Quebec, the textile mills in the Ottawa valley, the tanneries at Kitchener, Huntsville, Newmarket and Kingston. These are the industries which make up the profitable freight for our railway system. How much consideration has been given to them by the railroads during the past two or three decades? I see my furniture friend is in the house, and I shall include the furniture factories amongst the industries which go to make up the revenues of our railways. How much consideration has -been given to these industries? Very, very little. Apparently all the people can think of is wheat, coal, newsprint and similar commodities; no consideration has been given to the smaller industries in Canada. Many of these industries consume only four or five tons of one particular commodity and the result is that the purchasing agent in need of raw material is forced to take a carload lot of the particular commodity in order to obtain a respectable rate. This is in contrast to the situation which prevails in Europe, to which the hon. member for Kenora (Mr. Heenan) referred the other day. The minimum carload lot in this country is twenty tons, while in Europe the minimum is three or four tons. The purchasing agent finds that twenty tons of a particular commodity will stock his shelves for three or four months and it is necessary to tie up his capital for that length of time in order to obtain the carload rate. A similar condition prevails in 53719-187i
the shipment out of the. finished products of these industries. Shipments are made to sparsely populated districts and a shipment to a particular point may consist of only three or four tons. The industry finds it impossible to make up a carload shipment and in practically every instance the less than carload freight rate is almost double the carload rate plus one cent per hundredweight. This creates a real hardship for these industries. There is contained within the four comers of this bill an opportunity for the railroad companies to pool shipments offered for one particular destination. This will permit a reduction in the cost of operations and in the final analysis will accrue to the benefit of the shippers.
Heavy capital and renewal costs of these giant units of transportation must stop; these units are big enough now. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, who is so solicitous with regard to railway labour, said the other day during the debate, and was rather proud to say it, that within the last ten years these railways had been able to haul per man unit an extra 12,000 tons of freight. Every time you thus increase the efficiency, you cut out the man power necessary to operate the railways. The hon. member talks about efficiency, but if the efficiency rises from, let us say, 60 per cent to 80 per cent in the conduct of our railways and 90 per cent of that efficiency lies in the elimination of man power, where in the final analysis does the benefit accrue to the people of Canada?
We have followed the United States plan; we have Americanized the conduct of our roads and we have even surpassed the United States in that regard to an unnecessary degree. We shall have to put up with this, but the time'has come when we should call a halt to the extravagant expenditures of these big transportation services. We should stay where we are for a while till the population and production of Canada can catch up. In following the United States plan, we have just opened the gate, as it were, to motor truck competition; we have made it possible for motor trucks to fit into the groove where small industry was not getting any real service from the railway companies. It is true that the railway companies are now waking up tc the situation and mending their ways a little, but they are rather late in doing so. The handicap which has been placed on industry through the railway companies not meeting motor truck competition is something which the latter will not get over for some little time. The railway companies have been very arbitrary in setting up their classifications
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Harris

and freight rate structures. They seem to have followed the plan: Whatever the traffic will bear, that will be the freight rate. Let us take a case of goods originating in one point and being shipped to another point on another line of railway. If the other end was a competitive point, switching charges were absorbed; but if it was a non-competing point, switching charges were not absorbed. Was the cost in one case greater than in the other? This is a straight example of taking advantage of the local situation. In a like manner take cartage rates, these pin-pricking items of expenditure with which anyone in business finds himself confronted each and every day he is doing business with arbitrary bodies such as at times our railway companies have been and which, I hope, this cooperative measure now before the house will eliminate. One hundred yards from a railway station the cartage is four cents per 100 pounds; half a mile from the same point on the same car, it is still four cents and two miles from the same point it is still four cents. There is no equity, no consideration in that particular regard. At the present time they will quote you a freight and add cartage here and cartage there; in like manner the other Canadian companies will do the same, yet if you have, on a competitive line a siding into your plant, they will absorb the cartage. Is the cost any greater? In the past they have been able to put through these arbitrary rate rulings, and this cooperative measure is long past due in this country to establish and help out industry.
There are in the bill a few features to which I should like to address myself and perhaps only one in regard to which I should like to sound a note of warning. I am a little sceptical about subsection 2 of section 2 where it reads:
Parts II and III of this act shall not apply to any manufacturing, land, mining or ocean marine company, undertaking, property, work or service.
These particular units or assets of our transportation systems have in days gone by in their interlockings undoubtedly had a good deal to do with making our railway systems at some stage or another solvent. The converse of that is true that in days gone by our railway systems from their earnings have, to my mind, done a good deal towards stabilizing the solvency of some of these undertakings which the railway companies in their wisdom have seen fit to assume. During the last few years one might hazard a guess that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company has done a good deal to lessen or overcome the difficulties which the Canadian

Pacific might have had in the way of loss of revenue in the operation of their line. During the last decade they have been interlocking and when the railway company was not earning any money, perhaps the mining company or the land company or the mortgage transaction or the irrigation scheme or the immigration and colonization plan was. In other words, when one cow was not milking, the other gave a little milk. Now that these are being separated, my note of warning is to see to it that in days to come traffic borne on our Canadian railways will not be penalized in any degree for the benefit of these interests outside of the jurisdiction of this measure.
But if this one feature is something to which thought should be given in the days to come, there are many features of the bill of which I express hearty approval. We are getting back now to a sound financial statement from our railways. Section 12 of the bill provides that income deficits shall not be funded. Some of the older members will remember about ten years ago the late Right Hon. Mr. Fielding said in the house: "We have a credit balance in the national affairs of this country this year, but when we have to pay the deficits of the Canadian National Railways, it makes a debit balance and adds to the national debt." Mr. Fielding was sound in his bookkeeping system as far as the Canadian National Railways were concerned, and it was a matter of regret to me when I noticed that his followers in office did not continue that sound practice of writing off deficits as they occurred instead of putting them into capital account.
A continuous audit by independent auditors, in accordance with section 13, is something really worth while, but I am glad to see the rider which follows it to the effect that:
Their annual report shall call attention to any matters which in their opinion require consideration or remedial action.
That is very valuable. I would not be surprised if half the people of this dominion are not aware that the Canadian National Railways charge no depreciation whatever for the wear and tear of the equipment that is running on their rails to-day. This has not been done; it is not the bookkeeping practice of the system. I ask any hon. member who has had anything to do with business: Is it not sound business to have depreciation charges provided for each and every year? That practice, however, does not obtain in the bookkeeping of the Canadian National. It is too late to remedy this, yet I point it out as one instance among many others which

the auditors, if they do their duty according to this measure, must bring to the attention of parliament. The auditors' report attached to the financial statement of the Canadian National Railways has in years gone by been simply that two and two make four and that they have found this to be the case, but as a real audit it has been meaningless and the rider in section 13 will be a good thing for us in that connection.
As provided for in section 14, the annual report comes back to parliament and thus the bogey raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) some days ago is immediately dismissed. Of course we had to put in the provision to the effect that goods should be carried over Canadian railways to the Canadian seaboard rather than to foreign ports. I am quite in accord with that sentiment when it is placed within the four comers of the legislation. It should satisfy the qualms of conscience experienced by the hon member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) every time he looks at anything concerning railways.
What objection could there be to part III of the bill? It provides for the joint use of terminals, running rights over and joint use of tracks, and the avoidance of duplication in the construction of new lines. Hon. members know what the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) has in mind. We realize that if there were no branch lines there quite probably would be no trunk lines. There have to be branch lines to collect freight. But is there any harm in men who have the interests of the country at heart, the heads of the two railway companies, getting together and deciding on the use of one branch line rather than permitting that line to operate in opposition to another running parallel with it? Sensible men have the interests of Canada at heart, and are willing to cooperate. In his speech made at Winnipeg a few days ago Mr. Beatty indicated that willingness. Why would he not? If he is not willing, if the measure now before us does not go through this House of Commons, and if we continue the policy which has been in vogue during the last ten years, we are headed for a situation the result of which will be one of the greatest financial tragedies Canada has experienced in her economic history.
Then the bill advocates the joint use of facilities. In the city of Toronto we -have an example of what joint use means. The Toronto terminals are being used jointly and to the advantage of the people and the railways. In like manner I can picture possibilities throughout the length and breadth of Canada for the joint use of facilities for the common good.
I now come to part III of the bill, which concerns the pooling of freight and passengei traffic. As I have already spoken concerning this angle of the matter I shall not enlarge upon it at the present time. The hon. members for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) and Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) seem to be greatly worried about the elimination of services. For their information I direct their attention to subsection 5, section 9 of the bill, which states as follows: Subject to the terms of this act, and until otherwise provided or directed under its authority, every operation and service of .National Railways shall continue and be continued by all persons now concerned therewith as if this act had not been passed.
Surely that is sufficient to satisfy the minds of hon. members opposite. We are not going to dismantle the Canadian National Railways by cutting off services already enjoyed. We are not going to tear up a line here and another there, and leave without railway facilities the population who in good faith have settled in those parts. There is a clause in the bill dealing with that matter, and I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the issue has been raised by hon. members merely for the sake of having something to say. _
The principle behind this bill receives my endorsation. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has asked:	Why not send it
to a committee? I suggest that for eight or ten years the matter has been under consideration by the railways and shipping committee. Was it not before a committee of the Senate in 1925, and was it not again only recently before a Senate committee? Have there not been hearings of expert witnesses here and there throughout the length and breadth of 'Canada? Have not the hearings of the eighteen sittings of the Duff commission been put into print, both in the press and in the final report? Does he want to rethresh the old straw that has been threshed many many times? I wonder if it has occurred to him that every day that this House of Commons sits it costs the country $20,000? Will he dispute the fact that if the matter were sent to a committee of the house proceedings would be prolonged by at least another week?
So far as the high plane of debate is concerned, if it goes to a committee I assure the

hon. member it will be kept on that high plane. But, Mr. Speaker, some regard must be had for our friends of the fourth estate. Some hon. members, including the hon. member for Peace River, are worrying about compulsory cooperation. He has stated that we had the shoe on the other foot when we were talking about a compulsory wheat board. I say to him that the problems are entirely different from and foreign to one another. Anyone knows that in one instance we were dealing with 200,000 individual farmers, while in the present instance we are dealing with two corporate entities. Those two corporate entities will see to it that there is cooperation, and in my opinion when this legislation has passed and is functioning very little arbitral power will be exercised by the tribunal. Very few matters will be referred to it for decision. The men who are managing the two great railway systems want to ge,t together and cooperate. They realize where they are heading, and that it is in the interests of Canada and of themselves that they get together and bring our transportation problem out of the maze in which it is at the present time. They are ready and willing to cooperate, and as great Canadians, I am satisfied they will do so for the general welfare of Canada. With such cooperation I can picture a condition under which the present freight rate structure and freight rate classifications will'be made more flexible, thus 
having a tendency to obviate the possibility of cases such as those described by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Myers) where on account of freight classifications, bricks, mortar, window sash, cement and lumber cannot be loaded into one car. In the final analysis I am satisfied that the freight rate structure, which has remained at such a high level while other commodity prices have come down, will be lowered within a few years so that many primary commodities produced in this country will be able to reach the point of consumption. I have in mmd now the disadvantage of high freight rates so far as their effect on the tonnage of cur railroads is concerned. Not many months ago, I saw an offering of a million pounds of goods to go to Bermondsey, London, England, and when the cost of freight was calculated it was found to be more than the value of the commodity itself. I see that five hundred tons of goods are being burnt annually under the boilers of an industry in Toronto, displacing fuel which in turn would have been freight for the railway company. I see another picture, an industry that I pass each day when I am at home in Toronto, which last year produced two millions pounds of goods that found their market in Boston. Where are those goods going to-day? The low commodity value and the high freight rate to carry them to Boston have placed that thousand tons of goods under the boilers of that industry. With what result? The freight on the goods to Boston is lost, and also the freight on coal to that industry. Boston was supplied with the same commodity by waterborne traffic from South America. During the last twenty years-I can give the facts and figures-5,000 tons per year of nitrogenous products were shipped to Baltimore, that centre of industry which supplies the cotton growers of all the southern states. Now that entire 5,000 tons a year is being burned under the boilers of a 600 horse-power plant. With what result? Five thousand tons of freight haulage is lost to the railway, and the haulage of 1,500 tons of coal is also lost, on account of freight rates. The cooperation which is behind this legislation is going to do much in the years to come to help in an adjustment of that situation.

railways are to be amalgamated-or perhaps that is not the word; I will say they are to be "coordinated"; but what is going to happen when the Canadian Pacific Railway is unable to hold up its end? every person, high and low, rich and poor, aristocrat and bolshevist,-they are all forced into apartment houses, tenements and so on; every person is taken care of. for his country, and this is the way we recognize it." At one time I did think that this could be done. Now the prophecy is fulfilled: the lion and the lamb shall lie down together and a little child-the Minister of Railways-shall lead them.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. W. KENNEDY (Winnipeg South Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the house and which has emanated from the Senate is to my mind of first legislative importance in so far as the measures which have and which will come before us are concerned. It is of such importance to the city of Winnipeg, a constituency which it is my privilege to represent, that while I do not intend to speak at any considerable length, I feel my attitude might be misinterpreted in my own constituency if I failed to express my views before the bill goes to the committee of the whole.
Fifty years ago the city of Winnipeg was no more than a hamlet; to-day it is a city of approximately a quarter of a million. Fifty years ago there were no railroads either entering or emanating from that city; to-day a view from the air would show railroads branching out in every direction. There are the two transcontinental systems running east and west and other railroads fanning out north northwest, northeast and south from the city. We have in that city railway yards and shops which will compare favourably as to size, investment and number of employees with any other railway yard on this continent. An important part of our great railway system is the Canadian National Railway, with which this bill is concerned. This railroad is of importance not only from the physical and financial aspect but from the point of view of the number of employees to whom the purpose and effect of this bill are of primary importance.
It is unfair to say, as has been said upon certain occasions, that the government is not concerned primarily in the interests of the employees. I think it is a misstatement of fact to say that the first interest is either that of finance or that of the employees. The financial and physical aspect of the railways and their financial success is so closely correlated with the plight of the employees that it is senseless to endevour to separate them and say that either one or the other is of primary importance. Unless the railway systems of Canada can be made a financial success, there can be no permanent success for the employees. On the other hand, unless the employees are taken care of in a reasonable way you cannot make a success of any railroad, and particularly of any publicly owned system.
What are the objects of this bill? To put it briefly, they are to relieve the plight in which the Canadian National Railway now finds itself. But it goes further than that; it is an attempt to relieve the plight in which all the railways of Canada now find themselves, and particularly the two transcontinental lines, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. It has been suggested, I think by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), that it might be feasible and perhaps necessary to consider, the cutting down of the interest rates or even the paring down of the capital debt with respect to the moneys borrowed from the investing public in this and other countries. It seems to me that the road to success in the life either of an individual or of a great industry does not lie over the pathway of broken pledges or repudiated covenants. The government has put the people's money into this undertaking, the government appealed to the investing public in this and other lands to advance their money for the bonds of Canada upon the agreement to repay at certain rates of interest. To my mind it is unsound to argue now that these rates of interest are too high, it is unsound from the point of view of the country s honour and credit to argue that more money was borrowed than should have been borrowed, and on that basis to suggest repudiation. We must face the fact that these moneys, in whatever amounts they stand in the ledger, are moneys advanced by people who had faith in the resources of Canada and in the honour of this country.
To repudiate repayment of either principal or interest would be a dishonourable act so far as Canada is concerned, and I cannot believe it is the serious and considered opinion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that if perchance as prime minister leading a party he were face to face with the situation, he would draw a line through Canada's bonds and undertakings and announce to the world that she repudiated her pledges. If this were done, there might be a little immediate financial benefit, but after all the immediate present is only a very short period of time. Stretching ahead of every indivdual and of Canada is the long, long future, and it is better, even if we have to live a little plainer, even if we have as a nation to dig a little more deeply into our pockets, that Canada should honour her bond as given and pay her debts, as I believe she will.
What is the plight of the Canadian National Railways? It can serve no purpose to

enter into any detailed discussion. The facts have been placed on Hansard; they have been discussed on every public platform and in every newspaper throughout this country. The railways are facing a financial crisis. A description of the plight of our national railways was given by the first minister (Mr. Bennett) in his speech, concerning which statement there has been considerable comment in the house and also in the press. I refer to the observation made by the Prime Minister on the ninth of this month, when, describing the situation of the Canadian National Railways, he used words to the effect that essentially the people owned not the Canadian National Railways but merely the equity of redemption. The "equity of redemption" is essentially a legal term. To speak legally and in the narrow sense, it is true that the Canadian people do own the equity of redemption in the Canadian National Railways, but the conclusion drawn from that statement to the effect that the equity of redemption amounted to but little is incorrect.
What is the equity of redemption which the people of Canada own in the national railways? Let me explain this as simply and in as few words as possible. If I own a farm, borrow money on it and secure the loan by a mortgage, by the deed I mortgage to the person lending me the money my farm and all my rights and interest therein. If that mortgage be large and I fail to pay the interest thereon, and the interest and taxes accumulate to a degree that the amount of money owing under the mortgage is comparable, let us say, to the actual value of the land, it may be said with truth that I have little interest in that land. I have, it is true, the right to redeem it from the mortgage. That right to redeem is my equity of redemption. If all I own in this world is that farm; if it is mortgaged to the hilt and I do not pay and the mortgagee decides to realize, two courses are open to him. First, if it be the only asset I have; if my covenant be worthless; if to take a judgment against me in case of default would not realize the money, the mortgagee is driven to this position; he forecloses; he takes the farm and through legal means my equity of redemption is extinguished so that he owns the farm. It may be said that my equity of redemption from a practical point of view is worthless; but before he decides to foreclose and take over the farm, if he be a judicious man he will make inquiries to ascertain whether I have other assets available through which 
the amount of that mortgage may be realized. If he finds that I am competent to pay and he can make me pay, he will not foreclose the farm; he will make me pay. If I have the ability to pay and do pay, when I have paid I have my farm clear.
What is the position of Canada in respect to the national railways? The people of Canada, through the government, have mortgaged the national railways to the people who have advanced the moneys. Will those investors in Europe, the United States, Canada, foreclose and operate the road? No. What will they do? They will ask this question: Can Canada pay those mortgage bonds? I do not need to suggest the answer. Canada will pay those mortgage bonds through either the federal government or the provincial governments or both, and those bonds having been paid, the mortgage is paid and the railway belongs clear of encumbrances to the people of Canada. That is what the equity of redemption is worth in the Canadian National Railways, and it is of no small importance.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

When the
house rose at six o'clock I was referring to the interpretation placed by certain hon. members of the house, as well as by certain sections of the press, upon the expression used by the Prime Minister when he referred to the interests of the Canadian people in the Canadian, National Railways as an equity of redemption. I wish to recapitulate to the extent of stating that, in essence and in fact, the equity of redemption in the Canadian National Railways amounts to the Canadian National railway system free of all bonded debt- and I submit that is a very substantial interest. My reason for so stating is that behind the bonds of the Canadian National Railways in respect to borrowed moneys are the credit and the resources of the Canadian people. The Dominion of Canada cannot and will not default upon her bonded obligations, so far as moneys borrowed in connection with the Canadian National railway system is concerned.
Before leaving that subject I should like to make one further reference to some suggestions which have been made concerning repudiation of the bonded indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways, either as to principal or interest. Speaking on this subject

C.N.R,-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
I believe the hon. member for Ivenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) made the suggestion that it might be desirable to cut down the rate of interest on this bonded indebtedness, or even to wipe out all interest commitments-and this, Mr. Speaker, from a member of the house who at one time occupied a position as a minister of the crown, from a man who must have sat in council when many of these obligations were incurred. I submit that such a suggestion cannot come with good grace from the hon. member. Expressions of that sort, contribute nothing to the solution of the present problem. Canada will not repudiate. To the extent that such suggestions receive credence in this or any other country, to that extent instead of assisting to solve the problem they add to the difficulties we are facing by impairing the credit of Canada in the eyes of the world.
I wish now' to refer to another phase of the situation which I shall term the ghost of amalgamation. The possibility of amalgamation of the Canadian National Railways with the Canadian Pacific Railway has been suggested several times during this debate; but it was not first suggested here. I lived in the city of Winnipeg prior to the entry into that city of the Canadian National railway, and I can state that almost since that time there have been suggestions and rumours to the effect that fundamentally the Conservative party is friendly to the Canadian Pacific Railway and antagonistic to the Canadian National. Is that so? I ask for the proof. Has such propaganda been set on foot, and by whom? Not only has it been set on foot, but it has been persistently kept alive for one purpose, and one only, namely for political advantage. It has been the cry of the Liberal party, and has been kept alive by that party, its servants and agents and the press supporting it. That is not a figment of my imagination, but an actual fact. We who have to fight campaigns out in the west know at election times with what persistence the cry prevails, and we know the source from which it comes.
Oh, oh.
Hon. members may laugh, but they know I am stating facts.
It is certainly laughable.

Not as
laughable as the attitude of the hon. member. In 1930, when the present Prime Minister opened his campaign in the city of Winnipeg it was felt desirable that the propaganda to which I have referred should be given a definite and explicit denial. As hon. members know, that denial was given. On June 10,
1930, speaking in the city of Winnipeg and dealing with the question of the Canadian National Railways, the Prime Minister said, "No amalgamation." Perhaps it is too much to hope that in times of political warfare a definite statement given by such a public man who carries the respect, at least, of all Canadian citizens, would be a sufficient declaration. It has not been sufficient for those who still see in this ghost of amalgamation an instrument of political advantage.
A certain section of the press of the city of Winnipeg-I refer to it because with it I am more familiar-and of the press of other cities, has taken every opportunity to interpret any criticism of the management or operation of the Canadian National system as an attack upon that railway. But those criticisms have not been confined to the press. Despite the high plane upon which it was suggested this debate should be conducted, and despite the apparent unanimity of opinion that it should be so conducted, the same ghost of amalgamation was made to walk in this chamber. In fact it was taken for quite a ramble by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), and this afternoon, with a great deal of interest but very little conviction, I listened to remarks of a similar nature by the member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson). I heard him profess this afternoon, as he professes in nearly all his speeches, that he wanted to be fair and that he wanted to approach the subject with an open mind. I have no further comment to make than this, that if perchance an idea free from political bias ever found even temporary lodgment in the brain of the hon. member for South Perth it would find an atmosphere so inhospitable that it would come out like a bat out of hell.
I wish now	to refer to the	amendment introduced by	the right	hon.	leader	of theopposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). That amendment was professedly intended to force a declaration that there is no sinister purpose behind the bill and that there was no intention to amalgamate the two railways. I ask this house: Was	the right	hon.	leader	of theopposition really concerned with that? In half apologetic terms he prefaced his remarks by a statement to the effect that while probably he should accept the declaration of the Minister of	Railways	and	of the	Prime
Minister on the matter, yet to relieve fear and apprehension he had brought forward his amendment. I submit that in that action he was simply bringing up to date the old propaganda and giving new legs to the old ghost that the Conservatives intend to amalgamate
