the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways. I am here to-night to say, as I stated in Winnipeg at a considerable meeting of those definitely interested as employees of the Canadian National railway immediately before coming east to attend this session, that I had heard the Prime Minister declare in public against amalgamation, I had heard him so declare in private, and in caucus, and as far as I was concerned I was quite prepared to accept that declaration; but if they wanted a statement as to my stand on the matter, I was unalterably opposed to any proposal of amalgamation by this or any other government without a mandate from the people. That is my position.
What have we against this theory of amalgamation? We have the declaration of the Prime Minister in Winnipeg in June, 1930; we have the declaration of the Prime Minister in this house on the ninth of this month; we have the conviction of the rank and file not only of this party but of the party sitting opposite. It is not a question of the Conservative party being against the Canadian National Railways and the Liberal party for it, or vice versa. I submit the rank and file of all parties in this house are opposed to any proposition of amalgamation and would not tolerate it.
Let us make sure of it.

The only possible amalgamation that can ever take place would be when the people of Canada themselves decide that it shall be.
I now want to refer for a moment to the compulsory provisions of the bill. Part II of the bill provides for voluntary cooperation, part III provides for what might be termed compulsory cooperation. In criticism of these provisions it has been suggested that the two terms are incompatible, that you must not have the idea of compulsion associated in any way with the idea of cooperation. I do not propose to airgue that at length, but suggest this, that in all matters of cooperation there lies 'behind in some form or other, and intimately correlated, the idea of compulsion. The hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Young) shakes his head. Let me suggest this; in the great cooperative movement for the marketing of wheat in the west, read the contracts and tell me whether the element of compulsion is absent. In the cooperation of citizens to enforce the laws, take for example in the old land the speakers in Hyde park, why do they so seldom transgress the law? Why do they cooperate with the authorities to observe the law? Because they know and realize

that behind that voluntary cooperation there is force to see that the law is carried out. And while for academic purposes the opposition of compulsion to cooperation may be of some interest, it is only as a mental exercise.

It is not sound there.
Mr. KENNEDY" (Winnipeg):	Whether it
be sound there or not, to my mind it is purely an academic question and does not go to the root of the matter at all.
Now I come to the last division of the subject, that is this board of three trustees and the arbitral tribunal. It is true, as hon. members have pointed out, that the board of three trustees is vested with wide powers. I concede at once that to vest a board with such wide powers as are entrusted to this board is a matter of concern to the people of Canada and to this house, and to all who are interested in the success of the Canadian National Railways. As to the number, why three? It is open to argument; the number might be one or three or five, or seventeen as at present. But a royal commission spent considerable time investigating the whole subject, and they have recommended as best under the circumstances a board of three members. I do not suggest that because the Duff commission have recommended three, therefore it should be three. I do not suggest that they are in a much better position to decide than are members of this house. But after all, having made a thorough inquiry into the matter, having gathered such evidence as they could, the Duff commission have recommended three. And apparently that number appealed to the Minister of Railways, who was charged with the duty of introducing this bill into the house, and it appealed to the government. I have no quarrel with the number three. Had the government said five that would have been acceptable to me. But this principle I do think is sound, having regard to the purposes for which the board is being set up: that it should not be a large and unwieldy body. Seventeen is certainly too many. I would have no quarrel with five, but that does not mean that one should be opposed to three. The set-up of the board and the reason on which it is founded is financial, an executive setup- not geographic, not class representation. But with this I do agree, the principle of the statement which emanated from some hon. member opposite, that inasmuch as the Canadian National system is a publicly owned system operated for Canada and for Canadians, in the choice of that committee of three it is not a trivial matter but a matter of primary importance that the three who are

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
appointed to that tribunal shall believe in the principle of public ownership. As a private citizen you have a business the management of which you wish to delegate to someone; being interested in the success of that business, are you going to choose as manager or managing board a person or persons who believe in some other system than the one yon believe in?
Hear, hear.

I do not say that they shall be fanatics in the matter of public ownership, but it should be a board not handicapped at the beginning by lack of faith in the principle of public ownership.
As to control by parliament and by the people over this board, it has been urged that parliament is entirely divesting itself of any control. I submit that that is not correct. We have, as has been pointed out, parliamentary control by virtue of the power of parliament to withhold the grant of money. We have also this, and it should not be regarded lightly, that the same power which creates that board under this bill has power to change it.
Only with the consent of the Senate.

Well, the
two houses of parliament.

May I ask my hon. friend
a question? He has stated that parliament has control over the expenditures of the board. Where does he find that in the bill?

They must
submit their disbursements to parliament.

Not with regard to the
operation of the railroad-only for deficits and capital expenditure.

Well, that
is a very substantial amount.
Oh, oh.

During the
past year it amounted to somewhat around $70,030,000 and from present indications it would appear that it might be as much or more next year, perhaps $80,000,000.

What control does that
give us?

This control, that they cannot operate very well without money being voted. Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker, that parliament, which creates this board, can also legislate it out of existence. The hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) suggested that having appointed them for seven years parliament would not lightly disturb that arrangement. I agree that it should not do so lightly, but it must be remembered that if the board does not function as, in the opinion of parliament, it should function; if it does not work in the interests of the Canadian National Railways and of the Canadian people, I think no such consideration as a previous commitment by statute would or should stand in the way of further parliamentary enactments if such should be necessary.
I should like to conclude by referring to the rights of labour. It has been urged in this house that labour should have a representative on the board of trustees, and I may say frankly that so far as I am concerned I see no very sound argument against that being done. The employees of the railway are tremendously interested in the road and its success. Time will not permit me to enter into any detailed discussion of this question, but I wish to say here and now that I should he very happy indeed to see a representative of labour on that board.
Now Mr. Speaker, what are the chances of success? The success of the Canadian National Railways will depend upon sound management, and in my view the interests of labour will be served best if the railways can be made a financial success, thereby giving the employees both present and future assured employment instead of 'intermittent work. Success must be predicated upon the calibre of the board, upon their ability and their fairness in considering the rights both of labour and of capital. The success of the Canadian National Railways is predicated not only upon the material resources of this country but upon what might be called its spiritual resources as well; that is, the people themselves. We are a nation drawn from many peoples, with all that is best of all those races, and surely we can look with confidence upon that background. The Canadian people have an ancient pedigree which predicates success; in fact they have a veritable genius for success. To the Canadian people drawing upon such resources, success, while it may be delayed, cannot be permanently denied.

Mr. Speaker, I know my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy) will not expect me to follow his remarks at any great length. I should like to say that I think the character of the debate has indicated that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) believed, when he introduced this bill, that it was in the interests of the house and of the

country that this very important matter should be discussed in as non-partisan a manner as possible. I listened with interest to my hon. friend who has just sat down, and I may say to him that with many of his arguments I entirely agree. But, while adopting the very commendable attitude taken by hon. members on both sides of the house, I desire to say that his strongest argument was not his suggestion that the people of this country could feel sure there would be no amalgamation of the two roads because in his keynote speech the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) gave the pledge that amalgamation *would not take place. That, I submit, was not the most cogent evidence that it would not happen.
I entirely agree, Mr. Speaker, with my hon. friend's remark that in all probability the interests of the bondholders will be properly looked after. I must say that I do not take much stock in the great solicitude that has been expressed in this house, particularly by the Prime Minister, for these bondholders. What is their position? They hold bonds to the extent of SI,300,000,000, and to some of us that seems a very large amount of money. No doubt it is, but the Prime Minister also stated that the people of Canada have SI.000,000,000 invested in this road, money they have actually paid out, but for which they do not hold bonds. For security the bondholders have not only the assets of the road but also the guarantees and the resources of the people of Canada, and I quite agree with the statement that bondholders could have no better security than the guarantees of the various provinces and of the dominion. So I think we need not lose any sleep over the possibility of the bondholders losing money. But was the argument of the Prime Minister as to the bondholders really being the owners of this road correct? W'as his analogy between these bondholders and the investors in a company whose concern has gone into liquidation a proper one? Ordinarily the company which has gone into liquidation must realize its assets. A number of hon. members were on the committee to which I had the honour to belong a year ago considering amendments to the Bankruptcy Act. The evidence brought out there disclosed the startling fact that in the previous year the claims made against bankrupts in this country amounted to over $58,000,000, while the assets realized amounted to something like $14,000,000, of which amount less than $4,000,000 in actual cash reached the creditors. I think there is not much analogy between the creditors who received $4,000,000 out of $58,000,000 and the bondholders who

will be paid every dollar owed them under those bonds.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer for a moment to the statement made by my hon. friend with regard to the circulation of Liberal propaganda. I hope that if such statements have been made they are quite incorrect. But I do not agree with my hon. friend from Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), who spoke this afternoon, with regard to the wisdom of amalgamation. I do not think it is desirable. I must take an opposite attitude from that of my good friend but on exactly the same grounds.
What is the situation that has brought us into the position which the people of Canada find themselves in at the present time? I would mention a fact which I think is well known in this house, and it is this, that railway difficulties in Canada are by no means a new problem. There is not a member in this house who does not know that ever since confederation one of the great problems of the Canadian people has been the railway problem. That has been with us always, and I am glad to observe, listening to remarks made from all corners of the house since this debate began, that the members of this house are about as nearly in accord at the present time as they have ever been in the history of the country. And that should be so, because if there ever was a time when all parties in the house and in the country should endeavour to discuss problems with an eye single to the interests of the people of Canada as a whole this is the time.
It is impossible to discuss anything with the Prime Minister.

Well, he is not here at
the moment-

He is never here; he
should be here.
Order.

Throughout the time that these problems have presented difficulties to the Canadian people we have always had someone who was honest and sincere in being very pessimistic about the outlook of the Canadian railways; but looking back on what has occurred I think we can all be very thankful that throughout that period there was always someone with vision and faith enough in the future of the country to take an optimistic view. Mistakes have been made, it would be impossible in a matter of this kind that mistakes should not be made; but we must not forget that one of the greatest achievements in the history of the country is the increase which there has been

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Elliott
in the trade of Canada during the present century. I should like to give some figures, if the house will bear with me, which I submit are very important if we are to .understand just why the trade of Canada became as great as it was and the prosperity of this country correspondingly great. I would refer to one branch of what I think is the greatest industry in Canada; that is, one department of one branch, the wheat growing industry, in order to show its effect on the railway problem and the effect of the railway problem on wheat-growing in the dominion. Let me put a few figures on Hansard to indicate how the railway development in this country has contributed to that great industry.
In 1901 we exported 9,000,000 bushels of wheat for which we received $6,000,000. Now, if my hon. friends will bear in mind these figures they will appreciate the extent to which wheat growing and agriculture generally have benefited in this country through railway construction. In 1911, we exported 45,000,000 bushels for which we received $45,000,000. In 1921, ten years later, we exported 129,000,000 bushels and received $310,000,000; in 1931 we exported 217,000,000 bushels for which we received 8177,000,000; and in 1929, which was the largest year in our exports, we shipped out 3/0.000.000 bushels, for which we received $428,000,000. I will give one or two more figures before I leave that phase of the subject. In the ten years from 1901 to 1910, we exported an average of $27,000,000 a year; for the next decade $145,000,000 a year; and for the last decade, $297,000,000 a year.
These figures are, I submit, the best evidence that can be given to this house and the country with regard to the effect which railway development in Canada has had upon this branch of the great agricultural industry. In the twenty years, from 1911 to 1930 inclusive, we received for wheat exported from Canada $4,430,000,000. That is for wheat alone; and it has been due very largely to the creation of new wealth in agriculture that Canada has made such tremendous strides in the present century. To-day the best wheat and oats produced in the world are produced four hundred miles north of our southern boundary; they are produced in a region where twenty years ago it was supposed that wheat of any kind would not grow.
Recently wheat has been at its lowest price in several hundred years. The freight on low grades has been in some cases greater than the total amount received by the farmer. Out of what he received he had to pay interest, the cultivation of land, the seed, harvesting, threshing and hauling to the station. A large percentage of that wheat has been produced
in western Canada, and if it had not been for the foresight and vision of the men who through good report and evil report had faith enough in this country to build lines of railway, perhaps beyond the requirements of the country, more than half of that great wheat production would not have taken place. Even in prosperous times wheat cannot be produced far from railways. Various causes, into which I will not enter to-night, have contributed to the low prices for agricultural products. As I say, I do not propose to discuss these at the present time, and I am free to admit that there is a limit to the amount of foodstuffs that can be consumed at any given time. The world to-day seems to have reached that limit. There is no doubt however that the time will come, and we hope quickly, when Canada will again be on the road to prosperity, when the demand for products of the Canadian farm, forest and mine will again be extensive outside of this country. When that time comes our railways will do a business comparable to that which they did in 1928, when my hon. friend the Minister of Justice took such great credit for the part his party had taken in the building up of the great organization known as the Canadian National railway system.
It is bad policy for any concern to determine its future by conditions as they exist either at a time of great depression or at a time of great prosperity. There is no doubt about it, we must economise; that is forced upon us. It is ubter folly to talk of spending money which you have not got and which you cannot get. I think every hon. member is in agreement with that portion of the report of the commission which deals with the necessity at the present time for practising economies. However, I do not think that this is the time for the people of Canada to lose faith in their country and to begin to believe that pants of our great railroads should be scrapped or that other radical changes should take place simply because we are now suffering a depression in common with all the rest of the world
I should like to direct the attention of the house to the fact that the position of the railways of this country is much better than the position of the country as a whole. If the railways are bankrupt then I would not like to say just what is the exaot position of the whole country. I desire to give a few figures to show what the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific have done in miles of tonnage and number of passengers carried during recent years. In this respect I find that the railways have done much better than most of the branches of the government. For the twelve months ended January 31,



C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Elliott
1930, our domestic exports were $1,160,000,000, while for the year ending January 31, 1933, they were $487,000,000, just a little over a third of what they were three years previously. Our imports were reduced in about the same proportion. The customs duties for the year ending January 31, 1930, amounted to. $205,000,000, while for last year they amounted to $84,000,000. In 1930 they were about two and one-half times what they were three years later. If we are going to come to the conclusion that the Canadian National Railways are doomed, I think these figures offer the best evidence that many other institutions, including the present government, are also doomed.

What a difference! None of that was said the other night, because at this time it is not in such good form or fashion to boast of having been such good friends of the Canadian National; at least that is the attitude of our hon. friends opposite. Let me finish the quotation:
We have now spent more than $100,000,000 upon that undertaking.
Note this.
These railroads were not roads that could compete with the Canadian Pacific system, and so we had to spend hundreds of millions of dollars upon the system to make it efficient and effective.
That was said at the same time in 1928.
What is the history of the amalgamation of those two roads? I know there are many complicated facts, but we can summarize them. The Dravton-Acworth report was

brought down in 1917 recommending that the government take over the roads, particularly the Canadian Northern. The Canadian Northern got into difficulties. The government purchased the stock and under arbitration paid 810,800,000 for stock that is said not to have been worth a cent. It paid for the stock and it had to assume the bonds as well. What did the government do? Do my hon. friends from the maritimes remember what it did? It established Mr. D. B. Hanna, chairman of the Canadian Northern board, as director of the Canadian Northern Railway, and at the same time it put the Canadian Government Railways under Mr. Hanna as well and moved the headquarters of the Canadian Government Railways with the Canadian Northern Railway to Toronto. That was in 1917. We went along for a while with Mr. Hanna running from Toronto the Canadian Northern and also the Canadian Government Railways. Then the situation arose that the Grand Trunk fell down on their guarantees in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. The result was that the Grand Trunk Pacific went into receivership and the Minister of Railways was appointed receiver. In order to give Mr. Hanna a little more to do, the minister made him and his board act for the minister as receiver of the Grand Trunk Pacific. So we had Mr. Hanna and his board operating the Canadian Government Railways consisting of the Intercolonial railway and the National Transcontinental railway, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk still was left out.
In 1918 and 1919 negotiations went on with the Grand Trunk; there were agreements, arbitrations and lawsuits, but finally in 1920, I think, an arrangement was completed whereby the Grand Trunk stock was acquired by the government and, as everybody knows, that stock was acquired under an arrangement whereby it would be valued at arbitration. The arbitrators finally met and with the late Chief Justice Taft dissenting, found that the stock had no value whatever. The Grand Trunk directors were still allowed to direct. In 1921. I think it was. a Canadian board was appointed by the Grand Trunk and then we had Mr. Hanna running the majority of the roads of which I have spoken and the Canadian Grand Trunk board under Sir Joseph Flavelle running the Grand Trunk Railway. In order that there might be coordination-and this is the first instance we have had of an arbitral tribunal-we find a committee of management appointed of which Mr. Kelley of the Grand Trunk was chairman. That committee operated for a year or more
trying, if possible, to coordinate the operations of those two railways. As a matter of fact the coordination was not particularly successful. It is referred to in one of the minister's reports near the end of his regime and if I have time, I shall put it on record. The Hon. J. D. Reid was, I think, minister at the time and he makes this report:
The system of joint management was stated by the minister to be embarrassing, inconvenient and expensive though justified as a temporary expedient and as providing for the ixjssession which the company (the Grand Trunk) should have during the preparatory period of its case and, at the same time, by means of a committee of management, for such a measure of unification with the government railway system as might be possible.
When the Grand Trunk stock was acquired, and the control by the management committee set up, government ownership of railways was virtually accepted. In fact the Duff report says on page 13 that the government of the Dominion of Canada was projected into the railway business in 1917. It states:
Government ownership of railways on a large scale as a national policy was not contemplated or planned by any government and was not submitted for adoption to the people of Canada. But when in 1917, the government refused to permit the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to negotiate for the majority shares of the Canadian Northern, there was practically no escape from government ownership of all the railways now comprised within the Canadian National Railway system. The consequent completion and operation of the hitherto privately owned and operated lines with the publicly owned railways followed as a matter of course. Thus by a combination of contractual obligations and parliamentary measures, the country was projected into the railway business on a large scale.
I am quoting from the Duff report at page 13. This is what it says in contrast to the offhand and rather casual reference which my hon. friend made the other night inferring that it was the government of my leader that was in power when the railway complication took place. Nothing had been done in

No wonder the present Minister of Justice in 1929 was loud in his praises of the railway system. It is impossible to quote too often his remarks, w'hich have already been quoted in this debate. They are as follows:
Now, when this wonderful Canadian National railway system has more than justified itself, now that it is rapidly becoming in the nature of a great national asset, now that we may look forward to a day not perhaps in my life time, but in the life time of some here, when this system will start repaying the government of Canada part at least of the money it owes to the treasury, to the day when it will have a clean sheet as it ultimately will have, in regard to its bonded indebtedness to the public; now that the system is in this, a thoroughly prosperous condition, this government desires to treat it as its own creature. Let me say, in concluding my remarks on this phase of the subject, that the national railway system in this country constitutes a national monument to the ability and statesmanship and determination of a single man, a member of a former Conservative government, and subsequently Prime Minister of that government. It is to his ability and foresight, to his statesmanship and determination, that the people of Canada are indebted for this wonderful system of national railways.
The chickens come home to roost.

Yet within two years we have the Prime Minister of Canada comparing this railroad to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and saying we must have a receivership for it! I say that no more unhappy or misleading or harmful expression was ever used than to talk about receivership for the Canadian National. An hon. gentleman in another chamber the other day intimated that while they were the mothers of the road they did not much like the way the foster father had treated it the last six or seven years. Well, after the record I have given I think that this road would be willing to trust itself to the tender mercies of the foster father rather than to the careless and indifferent and inconstant mother who now seems to care so little for her offspring. Receivership, my right hon friend says! He might just as well talk about the government of Canada being in receivership. We have a deficit of $200,000,000 or more; does that mean we are going into receivership? The situation is that we are paying our interest as usual; there is nothing to go into receivership about that I know of. You have a receivership when you do not pay your interest. The people of Canada are paying this interest and propose to pay it. I submit my right hon. friend used an expression extremely harmful to the Dominion of Canada. One would think, Mr. Speaker, that there was $2,300,000,000 of debt that we never had before. But when' we took over these roads there was over $1,700,000,000 due on them. Let me tell you how the $2,300,000,000 is made up. It is not any new figure. The amount due the public is $1,263,000,000, including unguaranteed debt; $618,000,000 dominion government advances, and $405,000,000 for Canadian government railways; $2,286,000,000. Of that $1,700,000,000 was on the time that we took the roads over, and as far as the Canadian National is concerned we have added in capital expenditures just as much and no more in percentage to mileage as the Canadian Pacific has spent during the past ten years. So that comparatively we are in exactly the same position, as far as capital expenditure is

concerned as we were in 1921. And yet a road which was spoken about in such wonderful terms in 1928, which has not done any worse, except that it has not made as much operating revenue, but which at the same time has not increased its capital expenditures any faster than the Canadian Pacific, is now talked about as going into receivership. Yet the people of Canada are in a position, and I hope always will be, to pay the interest.
What is the situation in regard to this road? That brings me to a point that it seems to me is overlooked-it may be regarded as bookkeeping, but I think it is essential if you are going to give the Canadian National system a fair chance. We are talking as if the Canadian National owed us $2,288,000,000. You might just as well say that the Post Office Department owes us $70,000,000 because the post offices and public buildings cost us that much. Do we ever expect to get interest on that? Certainly not. Do you ever expect to get interest on the cost of public works and public utilities all over this country? Certainly not. But because the roads which happen to make up the Canadian National system at some time in their career as private enterprises cost $2,286,000,000, we say this road is going to the demnition bow-wows because it does not pay interest on that amount. It was never bought to pay interest on that amount; the roads were bought as public utilities. The sooner we get these railways recapitalized so that they can be given a fair chance, the better it will be for the finances of the Dominion of Canada and the fairer for the railway itself. My friends have a perfect right to say: You were in power for nine years, why didn't you do it? I say to my hon. friends that it was repeatedly considered, and it was felt that we should have experience for a reasonable time in order to see just what this railway could do. I believe that now is the time this should be done, and particularly do I believe that it should be done when we are proposing to hand over this railway to a set of trustees who are going to run it economically and under a system to make it remunerative. That is the word used in the act. Remunerative on what? Are you going to require the trustees to run it to pay interest on $2,286,000,000? It has never done it yet. It paid interest on a portion for two years. The best estimate I can make, looking at the gross earnings year by year, is that if we get interest on perhaps $700,000,000 or $800,000,000 that would be fail to the railway and to the people of Canada. I submit we might just as well decide now that the people of Canada will cut their loss,

it it is a loss, in connection with the Canadian National, and do what almost every other concern is doing, have a reorganization, cut down fixed charges and give this railway a chance to live and pay its way. I cannot conceive how you are going to put trustees in charge of this road and tell them to run it on the principle laid down in section 16, "remunerative operation," without fixing some decent amount of capital on which the railway is supposed to pay interest. Mr. Speaker, in spite of all that has been said I feel it my duty to express my views with regard to the bill which is now before the house, because in my opinion this is the most important measure to be considered this session. First we had what is supposed to be a very serious railway problem. The government, realizing the gravity of the situation, appointed a commission, and now we have this bill which is based upon the report of that commission. I will not go into further detail.
My first reason for opposing this bill is that it does not suggest any solution of this great railway problem. More than that, however, I fear that it does mean a consolidation of the two railway systems, probably for all time to come, through the provision concerning the leasing of part of the Canadian National system to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I come from a part of the country which is served almost equally by the two great systems, in the main by branch lines though part of the main line of the Canadian National runs through my district. I hold no brief for either system, but I am concerned over the possibility that through the consolidation of these two systems there may be more men out of work than we have at the present time. I am also fearful that this leasing I have mentioned will result in the branch lines suffering severely through whatever efforts may be made in the name of economy. I am afraid that the Canadian National system may become completely submerged in the privately owned company before many years go by, and to such an extent that it will not be able again to operate as a separate entity. Now, the opinion that the Canadian National railway system may not be able to function as a separate entity is not my opinion alone; we have the opinion of Sir Joseph Flavelle, one of the commissioners. In reply to a question asked by Mr. Beatty he used these words:
We are legislating for the future needs of the country, and the adoption of your suggestion would mean one system of railways in this country for all time to come, unless parliament intervened and said, "It is intolerable; we will break it up." ... I am not altogether sure of the capacity of its executive to interpret, without the whip of competition, what the public have a right to secure in the way of service. . . .
That is the opinion of Sir Joseph Flavelle with respect to this problem, and I say with him that we do indeed need the whip of competition if the people are to get that service they are entitled to. Another thing which the government seems to have lost sight of entirely is the fact that these railways were not built exclusively for the purpose of making money, but as a public utility. Nor did the
railways themselves take that view, that they were operating solely for the purpose of making money for the country.
I will direct attention to the branch line problem, and I will do so as briefly as I can.
I believe that railway development and progress in the direction of branch lines was largely responsibile for the fact that for a number of years our railway operation was so-successful, as pointed out by the previous speaker. From 1923 to 1930 the branch lines .unquestionably played a very important part in providing tonnage for the main lines. On that account it seems reasonable to me to conclude that the development of the country itself has been very materially assisted by the policy of the railways in building branch lines ahead of settlement. Had it not been for this, this country would not have attained the success it did, nor would it have made such strides during the years from 1923 to 1930. This being true, and in view of the fact that the railways themselves did not take the view that they were operating entirely for the purpose of making money, but also had regard for the welfare of the people of Canada in the extension of branch lines, I wonder why it is that the supporters of the government in this house are to-day criticizing our railways to the extent they are. Why is it that the railways are being so severely criticized, notwithstanding that practically every other utility you can mention is in just as bad a position financially as the railways?
Let me refer once more to the evidence taken before the Duff commission. In this connection I will read a few passages from the evidence of Mr. Hungerford, the acting president of the Canadian National Railways, given before the commission. He was pointing out the conditions of these railways when they became a separate entity under the management of Sir Henry Thornton, and he made this statement:
The situation which confronted the new management of the consolidated properties was an extremely difficult one and it had a great multitude of problems to solve. The Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern were not entirely completed nor equipped for operation and the earlier constructed lines of the latter company were in a very poor physical condition; while the Grand Trunk and Intercolonial were badly run down as a result of war pressure and financial limitations. All of these groups were very short of rolling stock and what was owned was generally in a poor condition of repair.
On practically all of the lines, the condition with respect to ties, rails, ballast, bridges, buildings, and other features of like character was most unsatisfactory; terminal facilities required enlargement and rearrangement to

tional transcontinental system. Nevertheless the Prime Minister at least pretends that he is in favour of both the trans-Canada highway and the St. Lawrence waterway.
I contend that the legislation now before the house is not necessary in any sense of the word. In the first place it will not solve the problem, and as a matter of fact I have not heard an hon. member opposite, supporting the government, claim that it will do so. I believe the government at this time should let the railways continue unmolested to do as they have been doing in connection with their cooperative measures. Let them cut down their expenditures as they have been doing. In 1932 the revenue of the Canadian National Railways was down $150,000,000 as compared with 1928, and during that period they reduced their expenditures by something like $100,000,000. If the government would change their policy so as to allow goods to move freely in and out of the country, the railways would get business, but under the present system that cannot be expected. If this legislation means the further consolidation of the two railways, as I believe it will, it will at the same time mean throwing more men out of employment and I do not believe any of us at- this time wants to see that happen. Because of the facts I have mentioned I am entirely opposed to this bill and for that reason I shall have to oppose it when it comes to a vote.
